title: I Failed My Classes. It Was the Best Thing That Ever Happened to Me.
content:
There was a version of me from last semester who would have never let that title exist.
That version had a 3.9 GPA, never missed an assignment, was grinding research, holding down a part-time internship, and trying to build a startup on the side. I wore the chaos like a badge of honor. I thought I was built different — some kind of academic weapon who didn't have to choose.
Something had to give.
This semester, it was my grades.
I had to take a W on one class. And it looks like I'm not going to pass another. A few months ago, that sentence would have broken me. But here's the thing — I'm not sad about it. I'm genuinely grateful.
Because failing taught me something that a 4.0 never could: I'm not a superhero. I'm a human. And humans have limits.
For so long I thought time management meant doing everything — just faster, just harder. What I actually needed to learn was how to prioritize. Not every class, every assignment, every opportunity deserves the same version of you. And when you try to give 100% to eight things at once, you're really giving 12% to everything.
Letting go of the academic perfectionism didn't break me. It freed me.
Right now I'm happier than I've ever been. I just got back from Japan. My internship at Liberty kicks off in about a month, and I'm meeting my manager on Thursday — and I'm excited, not anxious, not burned out. Just genuinely excited.
The startup work feels more focused. The things I'm building actually mean something to me now, because I chose them over other things. That choice has weight to it.
If you're a student trying to do it all — the grades, the internship, the side project, the research — I'm not going to tell you to quit. I'm just going to tell you: pick your thing. Go all in on it. And don't be afraid of what you have to let go of to get there.
Failure isn't the end of the story. Sometimes it's just the plot twist that finally points you in the right direction.
preview: How losing my GPA helped me find my priorities — and why I've never been happier.

title: What Japan Taught Me About Systems Thinking
content:
I just got back from Japan. And I came home a better engineer — not because I was coding the whole time, but because I wasn't.
Japan has this reputation for being intense. Work hard, be disciplined, respect the process. And that's all true. But what actually hit me wasn't the work ethic — it was the design of everything around it. The way the culture balances intensity with rest, individuality with collective consideration. The way the whole country, from its transit systems to its convenience stores, just... works.
That's when it clicked for me: Japan isn't just a culture. It's an architecture.

Every System Has a Contract
One of the first things you notice in Japan is how considerate everything is — not in a soft, passive way, but in a deeply intentional way. Quiet train cars. Designated smoking areas. Trash cans that only exist in specific places, yet somehow the streets are spotless.
This isn't compliance. It's a social API.
Everyone operates with an implicit understanding of their role within the larger system. You don't need a sign saying "be quiet" — the contract is understood. Each component trusts the others to hold up their end of the interface.
In software, we call this a well-defined boundary. The best-architected systems aren't the ones with the most enforcement — they're the ones where every service knows exactly what it's responsible for, and nothing more. Tight contracts. Minimal surface area. No one bleeds into someone else's domain.
When your components are that well-defined, the system becomes predictable. And predictable systems are fast systems.

Work Hard, Play Hard — and Why That's Actually a Systems Principle
There's a concept in Japan called ikigai — roughly, your reason for being. Your purpose. And what strikes me about Japanese work culture isn't just the discipline, it's the intentionality. Work is work. Rest is rest. There's a reason izakayas are packed on Friday nights — people actually decompress. They switch contexts completely.
Software engineers talk about context-switching as a tax. And it is. But there's a deeper systems concept here: isolation.
The most resilient architectures are the ones where failure in one domain doesn't cascade into another. A database going down shouldn't take out your entire application. A bad deploy in one service shouldn't corrupt another. You build walls not because you distrust your components, but because you respect the integrity of each one.
The Japanese version of work-hard-play-hard isn't sloppy context-switching — it's true isolation. When you're working, you're fully in that context. When you're off, you're fully off. No half-states. No undefined behavior.
Engineers who can't truly rest are engineers running without garbage collection. Eventually, memory leaks.

Kaizen: The Feedback Loop as a First-Class Citizen
You can't talk about Japan and engineering without talking about kaizen — continuous improvement. It's the philosophy behind Toyota's production system, and it's been borrowed by every agile framework since. But most engineers treat kaizen like a retro buzzword.
The real insight is architectural: feedback loops should be first-class citizens in your system design, not afterthoughts.
Most systems are built to do things. Fewer are built to learn things. But the systems that scale — the ones that survive — are the ones that can observe themselves, catch their own drift, and self-correct. Observability isn't a DevOps checkbox. It's the difference between a system that degrades silently and one that tells you it's struggling before it falls over.
Japan's infrastructure doesn't just run well because it was built well. It runs well because the feedback loops — maintenance schedules, civic reporting, cultural norms — are baked into how the system operates. Improvement isn't a sprint. It's a property of the system itself.

Bring It Back
I came back from Japan not with a list of tourist highlights, but with a mental model I keep returning to:
The best systems — cultural or technical — are the ones where every component knows its contract, isolates its state, and participates in its own improvement.

{{img:/images/posts/1773088569099.jpeg}}

That's not a Japanese idea. That's just good architecture. But sometimes it takes stepping inside a system that actually works to finally see it clearly.
Now I'm back. Building. And I'm thinking about my systems a little differently
preview: The country runs like a well-architected system. Once you see it, you can't unsee it.

title: I Go to a School You've Never Heard Of. I Still Got Interviews at Bloomberg, Capital One, HubSpot, NVIDIA, Jane Street, Liberty Mutual Lockheed Martin and way more
content:
I'm a sophomore. My university doesn't have a target school pipeline. No recruiters camping out at our career fair. No alumni network feeding into Wall Street or Silicon Valley. If you Googled my school, you'd probably move on in three seconds.
And yet: Bloomberg. Capital One. HubSpot. NVIDIA. Jane Street. Liberty Mutual. Lockheed Martin.
I'm not saying this to flex. I'm saying this because when I was a freshman, I genuinely believed the school you attended determined the opportunities you could access. I was wrong. And I want to be specific about why, because "believe in yourself" is not advice.

What Actually Moved the Needle
1. My GitHub Was My Real Resume
Recruiters at big companies see thousands of resumes. Most of them are identical: same bullet points, same buzzwords, same GPA padding. What they don't see every day is a sophomore with a GitHub that actually shows them you can build things.
I stopped treating projects as resume fillers and started treating them as products. Every repo had a README that explained the why, not just the what. Screenshots. Architecture diagrams. Deployment links where I could manage it. I wanted anyone who landed on my profile to understand what I built and why it mattered in under 60 seconds.
Your GitHub is a portfolio. Treat it like one.
2. Startup Experience Signals Things a GPA Can't
Before any of these interviews, I was already working on a startup. Unpaid. Nights and weekends. And I'll be honest: there were moments I questioned whether it was worth it.
It was worth it.
Not because of the equity, not because it's going to make me rich, but because it gave me stories that GPA kids can't tell. I could talk about making real architectural decisions with no senior engineer holding my hand. I could talk about shipping features to actual users and watching them use it. I could talk about what happens when something breaks in production and it's just you.
That is rocket fuel in a technical interview. Senior engineers don't want to babysit someone who only knows how to pass tests. They want someone who has felt the pressure of real stakes and kept building anyway.
3. LeetCode, But With Intention
I'm not going to pretend grinding LeetCode isn't part of the game. It is. But there's a version of LeetCode grinding that prepares you for interviews and a version that just racks up solved problems without understanding.
I focused on pattern recognition over volume. Once you truly understand sliding window, you don't need to memorize thirty sliding window problems. You need to see the shape of the problem and know which tool to reach for. I drilled the fundamentals hard: trees, graphs, dynamic programming, recursion. And I practiced explaining my thinking out loud, because the algorithm is only half of what they're evaluating.
Communicate your thought process. Always.

The Honest Truth About Unknown Schools
Here's what I've come to believe: prestige is a shortcut for lazy evaluation. When a recruiter sees MIT on a resume, they skip a few mental steps. When they see a school they don't recognize, you have to do that work yourself, upfront, through your projects, your experience, your presence online.
That's not unfair. That's just the game. And once you understand the game, you can play it.
The students getting filtered out from unknown schools aren't getting filtered out because they're less capable. They're getting filtered out because they're playing by rules that were written for a different type of candidate. Build in public. Put your work where people can find it. Make it impossible to ignore you.

A Note on Unpaid Startup Work
I get asked about this a lot. Is it worth working for a startup for free?
My answer: it depends on what you're getting paid in.
If you're getting paid in real responsibility, real ownership, and real learning, that has a dollar value that some paid internships can't match. I learned more from six months of unpaid startup work than I did from coursework in the same period. I made decisions that mattered. I shipped code that real people used. I failed fast and fixed faster.
But be honest with yourself about what you're actually getting. If you're doing grunt work for someone's half-baked idea with no equity, no mentorship, and no autonomy, that's not an investment. That's just free labor. Ask yourself: will this make me better? Will I have a story to tell because of this?
If the answer is yes, do it. The compounding on real experience is insane.
If the answer is no, walk.

You Don't Need Permission
No one is going to recruit you out of obscurity. No one is going to find your potential and hand you an opportunity because you have a good heart and work hard. You have to put the work somewhere visible, tell a story with it, and go get the thing you want.
Your school is not your story. What you build is.
preview: Your school's name is not your ceiling.

title: The AI Paper That Changed How We Build Docere
content:
{{img:/images/posts/download.png}}

A few months ago, a paper came across my feed that made me stop everything I was doing.
The Darwin Gödel Machine, published at ICLR 2026, describes a system that does something most AI researchers said was years away: an agent that rewrites its own code, tests each modification against a real benchmark, and keeps an archive of every variant that improved performance. Darwinian selection, applied to agent design itself.
The result was a coding agent that improved its own SWE-bench score from 20% to 50% — autonomously. No human intervention. No retraining. Just a loop: try something, measure it, keep what works.
I read that and immediately thought about classrooms.

The problem with every AI tutor on the market
ChatGPT is the same tutor today as it was a year ago. So is Khanmigo. So is every AI tutor I've seen.
They don't get better at teaching. They get better at sounding like they're teaching — through prompt engineering, RLHF, model upgrades. But none of them close the loop. None of them ask the only question that matters:
Did the student actually learn?
That question haunts me. I've spent two years building Docere, an AI tutoring platform deployed in two Minnesota middle schools with 500+ students. I've sat in classrooms. I've watched students interact with AI. And the thing that kept bothering me was this:
We had no way of knowing if our tutoring strategies were actually working — not in a "the student said they understood" way, but in a "their grades went up and they retained the material three weeks later" way.
The DGM paper gave us a framework to solve that.

What "benchmark" means in education
In the original paper, the benchmark is SWE-bench — a set of coding tasks with clear pass/fail criteria. The agent modifies itself, runs the benchmark, and measures the delta. Simple.
Education doesn't have that. Or at least, people assume it doesn't.
But we realized something: if your AI tutor is connected to a real Learning Management System — and ours is, through direct integrations with Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard — then you do have a benchmark. You have quiz scores. Assignment grades. Engagement data. Submission patterns. You have real, measurable outcomes tied to real students in real courses.
The question becomes: can you trace those outcomes back to the specific tutoring interactions that preceded them?
At Docere, the answer is yes. We've been building toward this for over 40 weeks.

A tutor that teaches itself to teach
I won't get into the full technical architecture — we have a research paper in progress for AIED 2026 in Seoul that will cover that properly. But here's the idea at a high level:
Docere doesn't use one fixed tutoring approach. It maintains a population of teaching strategies. Each strategy represents a different way of guiding a student through a concept — different questioning techniques, different levels of scaffolding, different ways of connecting new material to what the student already knows.
After every tutoring session, the system evaluates: did this interaction move the needle? Not "did the student say they understood" — did their actual performance improve?
Strategies that consistently lead to better outcomes get prioritized. Strategies that don't get phased out. And new variations get introduced, tested, and either kept or discarded.
Over time, the tutor gets better. Not because we shipped a new prompt. Because the system figured out what works — for different students, in different subjects, at different levels.
That's the part that gets me excited. This isn't a static product. It's a system that compounds.

Why this matters beyond Docere
The DGM paper is about coding agents, but the principle is universal: any AI system with access to a reliable feedback signal can improve itself through selection.
In education, that feedback signal has always existed — it's called a grade. We just never connected it to the AI doing the teaching.
I think this is where the entire AI-in-education space is headed. Not bigger models. Not better prompts. Closed-loop systems that measure what matters and evolve based on evidence.
We're not the only ones who will figure this out. But right now, with 500+ students, 10,000+ memories captured, and a research paper in progress, we might be the furthest along.
If you're interested in self-improving AI systems, education technology, or the intersection of the two — I'd love to hear from you. We're presenting at AIED 2026 in Seoul this summer, and we're always looking for collaborators, researchers, and people who think the future of education should be built on evidence, not vibes.
— Youdahe
preview: How a self-improving coding agent inspired a self-improving tutor.

title: I thought about github before tom preston
content:
I need to come clean about something.
Before I was born, I was a ghost.
Not like a scary ghost. More like a little floating idea ghost, drifting through the universe, just vibing. Collecting concepts. Putting them in my invisible pockets for no reason whatsoever.
And one day I floated past Tom Preston Werner while he was thinking really hard about something and I HEARD IT. The whole idea. Version control. Repositories. The whole thing.
But here is the deal. I thought of it first. By like half a second. Maybe a full second. I was a very quick ghost.
Except my version was not for code.
My version was for SOUP.
What if your grandma made a terrible batch of chili and needed to roll back to the previous commit. What if there were BRANCHES of the same stew. What if two aunts could open a PULL REQUEST on grandmas secret jambalaya and she could review it and leave comments like "this cilantro suggestion is not ready for production."
I tried to file a patent. As a ghost. As a prenatal soup-versioning specter floating around in 2005.
The patent office rejected me. No address. No social security number. No body.
Then I got born in 2006 and forgot everything instantly like a Windows XP crash with no recovery file.
Tom shipped in 2008.
Suspicious. Very suspicious.{{img:/images/posts/351d11dee112d732ad82699e1b2adb48.jpg}}

title: First Week at Liberty Mutual: Initial Impressions
content:
Wrapping up my first week at Liberty Mutual, I can already say it has been a really interesting start. Coming in, I had a certain expectation of what working at an insurance company would look like, but I have been genuinely surprised by how much it feels like a financial infrastructure company at its core.

There is a strong focus on systems, data, and how information moves through the organization. That gives everything a more technical and analytical edge than I expected. It is not just about policies and claims. It is about the underlying frameworks that make all of that possible at scale.
I am still getting ramped up, but the project I am working on lowkey feels like the perfect fit. It is something that is honestly a bit above my current understanding, which I actually really like. It gives me a solid benchmark to see how fast I can learn and grow. It is challenging in a good way and keeps me on my toes.

One of the highlights so far has definitely been the team. Everyone has been super welcoming and supportive, which made it easy to get comfortable quickly. There is a real sense of collaboration that makes a big difference.

Outside of work, I also got the chance to see the Hampton houses, and man these mfs are rich rich, like holy sh*t. Definitely a wild contrast and a reminder of how much money moves around in the spaces connected to this industry.

Overall, it has been a great first week, and I am excited to keep learning, keep pushing myself, and see where this experience goes.

title: carb maxxing might be the method
content:
i've been every size. 250 lbs, 140 lbs, and everywhere in between. i've done the cuts, i've done the bulks, i've tried basically every approach you can think of. and the one thing that consistently made everything worse every single time was cutting carbs.

workouts felt awful. energy was gone by the second set. i was grinding through sessions that should've felt good and just coming out feeling like trash. i thought that was just what cutting felt like. turns out i was wrong.

how i found out about carb maxxing
my friend brought it up a few weeks ago. he's been doing it for a while and kept telling me to just try it. i was skeptical  i'd been in the "carbs make you fat" headspace for a long time. but i figured i'd give it a shot.

the idea is pretty simple: keep carbs high, especially around training. your body runs on glucose. when you train, that's what it's pulling from. if you're depleted going into a session, you're working against yourself from the jump.

what actually happened
i'm not gonna sit here and say it's been some wild transformation. but lowkey my workouts have been noticeably better. i'm getting through sessions without hitting a wall. i'm not dragging myself to finish sets. the energy is just there in a way it wasn't before when i was keeping carbs low.

i always thought the sluggish feeling mid-cut was just part of the deal. like you're eating less so you feel worse, that's the trade. but i think it was specifically the low carb thing messing with my performance. calories were down but carbs were what was killing my training.

why i think low carb during a cut is actually bad
when you're already in a deficit, your body doesn't have a ton to work with. if you also tank your carbs, you're taking away the main fuel source for high-intensity work. your performance drops, your sessions get worse, and you lose the stimulus that was keeping muscle on in the first place. it kind of defeats the purpose.

keeping carbs up means you can still train hard even while eating less overall. you're not sacrificing performance to hit a number on the scale. and when training stays solid, the cut goes a lot better.

where i'm at now
i'm still figuring it out and i'm not claiming to have it all dialed in. but if you've been cutting carbs and wondering why everything feels so bad, it might just be that. try keeping them in, especially on training days, and see what happens. worked for me so far.
